title: Latent kinetic Ising models of neural spike trains
abstract: Inferring directed effective interactions from neuronal spike trains is a central inverse problem in statistical physics and computational neuroscience. Kinetic Ising models provide a tractable framework for this task, but their application to neural data typically requires binning spike trains into binary activity variables, discarding within-bin timing and conflating collective network dynamics with single-neuron history effects.   We introduce SpiKIsing, a latent-variable model that separates these two levels of description. A discrete-time asymmetric kinetic Ising model describes collective network activity, while continuous-time, history-dependent point processes generate the observed spikes conditional on the latent states, accounting explicitly for refractoriness and post-spike recovery.   We derive a variational mean-field expectation-maximization scheme in which the point-process likelihood enters as an effective observation field, enabling joint inference of latent activity, network couplings, and emission parameters. The framework extends naturally to maximum-a-posteriori inference with structured priors, including sparsity and a hierarchical extension favouring Dale-consistent outgoing interactions.   We validate parameter recovery on matched synthetic data and test the method on spike trains generated by a recurrent conductance-based leaky integrate-and-fire network. In this setting, SpiKIsing recovers sparse connection structure and correctly classifies all excitatory and inhibitory neurons despite the substantial mismatch between the data-generating dynamics and the SpiKIsing model.
summary: This work introduces SpiKIsing, a latent-variable model that separates the collective dynamics of neurons (modeled by an Ising process) from the continuous-time spiking process. It uses a variational EM scheme to jointly infer the underlying network couplings and emission parameters from raw spike data. The method is robustly validated, showing it can accurately recover network structure despite modeling mismatches.
main_problem: The paper addresses the inverse problem of inferring the directed effective interactions governing collective neuronal dynamics solely from recorded spike trains.
main_result: The proposed SpiKIsing model successfully recovers the sparse connection structure and correctly classifies neuronal types (excitatory/inhibitory) even when tested on data generated by different underlying dynamics.
method: It employs a variational mean-field expectation-maximization (EM) scheme to jointly infer latent network activity (modeled by an Ising process) and continuous-time emission parameters from the observed spike trains.
model_or_system: The system models neural spiking using a two-level latent variable approach: a discrete-time asymmetric kinetic Ising model governs the unobserved collective state, while continuous-time, history-dependent point processes generate the observed spikes conditioned on this latent state.
key_observables: Inferred coupling strengths (J), local fields (h), and emission parameters (e.g., $\lambda^+, \lambda^-$).
important_parameters: Latent time step ($\Delta t$), regularization strengths ($\gamma_1, \gamma_2$), and prior parameters ($ eta$).
main_assumptions: The primary approximation is using a variational mean-field approach, which treats the continuous-time point-process likelihood as an effective observation field for the discrete Ising dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the full generative mechanism, parameter recovery validation on synthetic data, and the final inferred interaction matrix compared to ground truth.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the latent variable model, derives the variational EM scheme, details the updates (including forward-only approximations), and validates the method using both synthetic and complex conductance-based LIF network simulations.
why_interesting: The framework uses concepts from statistical physics (Ising models, mean-field theory) to model complex, non-equilibrium biological dynamics, providing a rigorous mathematical structure for analyzing emergent collective behavior.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic representation of the SpiKIsing model. (Left) Latent trajectories for three neurons. Neuron i receives positive coupling Jij = 0.5 from neuron j, negative coupling Jik = −0.8 from neuron k, and local field hi = −0.1. The state of the presynaptic neurons at time t −1 determines the probability that neuron i occupies its active latent state at time t. (Centre) Emission layer, represented by the conditional point-process intensity of neuron i, with λ+ i = 10, λ− i = 0.5, τ abs i = 0.03, and ci = 0.01. Following the absolute refractory interval, the active-state intensity recovers according to ρi(δ) = δ/(δ+ci). (Right) A stochastic realization of the continuous- time spike...

Figure 1 illustrates the complete generative mechanism. Positive and negative incoming couplings respectively favour and suppress the activation of neuron i at the following latent time step. Conditional on the resulting latent trajectory, the emission layer generates individual spikes stochastically: active intervals are associated with a higher firing rate, while refractoriness and post-spike recovery determine the short-time structure following each spike. Thus the latent trajectory controls the collective dynamical state, but does not uniquely determine the observed spike times.

Figure 2: Matched-model validation of maximum-likelihood SpiKIsing inference. (a) Interaction recovery. Left: mean-squared error of the inferred interaction matrix as a function of the recording length T for different coupling strengths g. Right: inferred versus ground-truth couplings for three representative recording lengths. (b) Joint learning of latent and emission parameters. Evolution of the mean-squared errors in J, h, λ+, λ−, and c during inference. The inset shows ∆FnMF = FnMF(epoch) −FnMF(0). Simulation parameters are specified in the text.

Figure 3: Matched-model validation of sparse and Dale-structured MAP inference. (a) Sparse connectivity recovery. Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves for clas- sification of non-zero interactions at different recording lengths T. The inset shows the MSE of the inferred interaction matrix. (b) Recovery of Dale-consistent structure. Evolution of the neuronal-type classification during inference. The inset shows the fraction of ground-truth non-zero couplings whose sign is correctly inferred as a function of recording length T. Both experiments use networks of N = 100 neurons. Further simulation and inference details are given in Appendices E and F.
